## Proof

**Claim:** Every orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space is a Riesz basis.

**Definitions.** A sequence $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ in a Hilbert space $H$ is a *Riesz basis* if it is complete in $H$ and there exist constants $0 < A \le B < \infty$ such that for every finite scalar sequence $\{c_1, \dots, c_N\}$,

$$A \sum_{n=1}^{N} |c_n|^2 \;\le\; \left\|\sum_{n=1}^{N} c_n f_n\right\|^2 \;\le\; B \sum_{n=1}^{N} |c_n|^2.$$

Equivalently, $\{f_n\}$ is a Riesz basis if there exists a bounded, invertible (bijective) operator $T: H \to H$ and an orthonormal basis $\{e_n\}$ such that $f_n = T e_n$ for all $n$.

**Proof.** Let $\{e_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be an orthonormal basis of a separable Hilbert space $H$. We verify the Riesz basis inequalities directly.

For any finite scalar sequence $\{c_1, \dots, c_N\}$, by orthonormality $\langle e_n, e_m\rangle = \delta_{nm}$:

$$\left\|\sum_{n=1}^{N} c_n e_n\right\|^2 = \left\langle \sum_{n=1}^{N} c_n e_n,\; \sum_{m=1}^{N} c_m e_m \right\rangle = \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{m=1}^{N} c_n \overline{c_m}\,\langle e_n, e_m\rangle = \sum_{n=1}^{N} |c_n|^2.$$

Hence

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N} |c_n|^2 \;\le\; \left\|\sum_{n=1}^{N} c_n e_n\right\|^2 \;\le\; \sum_{n=1}^{N} |c_n|^2,$$

so the Riesz basis condition holds with $A = B = 1 > 0$.

Completeness of $\{e_n\}$ is part of the definition of an orthonormal basis (the closed linear span of $\{e_n\}$ is all of $H$). Therefore $\{e_n\}$ satisfies both requirements of a Riesz basis.

**Operator viewpoint.** Equivalently, taking $T = I$ (the identity operator), which is bounded ($\|T\| = 1$) and invertible with bounded inverse ($T^{-1} = I$), we have $e_n = I\, e_n$ for every $n$. Thus $\{e_n\}$ is the image of an orthonormal basis under a bounded invertible operator, confirming it is a Riesz basis.

**Conclusion.** Every orthonormal basis is a Riesz basis (with optimal Riesz bounds $A = B = 1$). $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
